newsitem.title: MEXICO: Under-par consumption seen leaving Mexico exposed.
newsitem.headline: Under-par consumption seen leaving Mexico exposed.

text.p: Morgan Stanley Dean Witter said on Monday it had bumped up its economic growth forecast for Mexico but warned that under-par expansion in consumer spending posed a threat to the healthy growth story.
"For 1997 we expect more growth (from 4.3 percent to 5.2 percent per annum). Growth in 1998 is raised from 4.0 percent to 4.5 percent," economist Chip Brown said in a research note.
He also revised forecasts for inflation and the peso, adding the unit would depreciate much more slowly than previously expected.
Lower mid-year inflation would bear down on the year-end total, he said, prompting a downward revision to 15.4 percent for the year compared with the previous 17 percent estimate.
He also sharply revised his peso forecasts a day after July 6 mid-term elections, predicting the currency would end 1997 at 8.3 pesos to the dollar compared to a previous forecast of 9.0.
He forecast an end-1998 level of 8.9 pesos to the dollar rather than the 9.7 previously predicted.

"All the revisions are constructive for the Mexico story -- a stronger peso, better growth and lower projected inflation," he said, adding the revisions came on the back of better than expected election results and in anticipation of a good second quarter corporate earnings season.

But while consumption spending growth was likely to increase a little more than expected -- May department store sales rose 8.0 percent in May and and retail sales rose 3.3 percent -- it was still failing to reach desirable levels, he said.
"There are risks to the Mexico story: consumer spending... is still below par and incomes are very compressed, which could threaten the growth story," he said.

He also warned that continuing strong capital flows could make the peso too overvalued, but discounted the possibility of political upsets after the July 6 vote which boosted the standing of opposition parties in the lower house of Congress.
"Political turbulence is possible as time passes, but there is general consensus on major policy issues," he said.
